gap: No result ChatGPT got states why the left and right channels fail outside the car at night (BlackboxMyCar: infrared light "is instantly reflected off the glass, resulting in a reflection or glare that will blind the camera"), nor what the hardwire kit that parked recording needs costs: $34.99 on the Vantrue N5S ($328.98 together), $39.99 on the Rexing R4 ($299.98 together), in the box on the $279.99 R4-RD.
standout_why: Compared against our own page (dealectric.com/best-4-channel-dash-cam, rank 1 in both chats), Dashlore's best-dash-cams guide and the Rexing store listings; Tom's Guide, Best Buy and the other ranked pages were not opened. Our page already says the side views are filmed from the windshield through the door glass, quotes Digital Camera World that "very little will be visible through the car's side windows" at night on the N5S, and says the R4, N5S and C4 hardwire kits are sold separately, with no price for any kit. It gives the effect, not the cause (IR reflecting off glass), and by its own summary does not discuss reflections or tint. Dashlore covers only the N5S, says "Parking mode needs a hardwire kit, sold separately" with no price, and says nothing on side windows or IR on glass. Rexing's listings state "4 infrared lights" per side camera but never say what happens when they face glass; its L4 listing claims the IR lights help "exterior views". The weak point is that the IR quote comes from a retailer's support page about rear windows, not from a maker.
decides: It splits the question by use. For parked side-impact coverage with everything under $300, the Rexing R4-RD ($279.99, Smart Hardwire Kit and motion sensor included) or the Rexing 4-channel bundle ($259.99 with kit, GPS and 64 GB card) fit; the R4 only just fits at $299.98 with its kit; the Vantrue N5S does not, at $328.98 with the 5-Level kit (or $323.98 with the $29.99 Voltage Display kit). The N5S stays under $300 only as a driving and rideshare camera, which is the segment it honestly wins: its IR cabin cameras light the seats with no glass in between. Any IR-equipped side lens turned to a door window at night works from ambient light alone, so the sensor matters more than the IR count for exterior views. I could not read the Botslab G980H page today (it is our linked 4-channel row), so whether its kit is in the box is still open; that decides whether it or the R4-RD takes the parked-coverage pick.

findings.value: "the infrared light is instantly reflected off the glass, resulting in a reflection or glare that will blind the camera"; "This will cause your videos to be overexposed or washed out."
findings.source_title: If IR cameras are better at capturing in total darkness, can I use them instead of standard rear cameras? (BlackboxMyCar support)
findings.note: A dash cam retailer's support article, not a maker; it is written about an IR camera mounted against the rear window. The page says "Updated 10 months ago" and does not mention tint. Applying it to side lenses turned to a door window is my inference from the same physics.

findings.label: Bitrate with all four channels, and what it fills
findings.value: DashCamTalk lists 14.3 + 9.8 + 9.8 + 14.3 Mbps = 48.2 Mbps at 30 fps per camera; that is about 21.7 GB per hour, so about 46 hours on a 1 TB card
findings.note: Arithmetic: 48.2 Mbps × 3,600 s ÷ 8 ÷ 1,000 = 21.69 GB/h; 1,000 GB ÷ 21.69 = 46.1 h. DashCamTalk lists the front at 2560 × 1440, while Vantrue's figure in our record is 2592 × 1944; the per-camera split came through a page summary and may be mis-assigned, the sum is what I rely on. Also lists capacitor, 1 TB max, parking modes "Buffered, Timelapse, Low Bitrate".
